background: In October 2024, news of a data breach exposing Burger King Russia customers broke following an August attack on the Mindbox marketing automation platform. The breach exposed 3.2M unique email addresses along with names, genders, dates of birth, phone numbers and approximate geolocations, with the data spanning 2018 to August 2024. Burger King Russia acknowledged the incident and advised it did not include payment or passport details.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 3,155,792 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Geographic locations, Names, Phone numbers.
editorial: The important boundary in this record is a marketing platform. Have I Been Pwned attributes the customer-data exposure to an attack on Mindbox and describes records spanning 2018 to August 2024. A person can appear in an old marketing dataset even if they no longer use the restaurant's account or app. The addition date in a breach index is also different from the date the incident occurred.

The source lists names, contact details, birthdays and approximate location, and reports the company's statement that payment and passport details were not included. That statement should not be expanded into either a guarantee that no other risk exists or a claim that cards were stolen. The listed fields can help make a fake loyalty reward or account-support message sound personal.

This is a risk interpretation, not a report of an observed follow-on scam. If you receive an unexpected reward or account message, open the official app or a known website yourself. A correct name or birthday does not authenticate the sender. Do not send a one-time code in reply or enter payment details through the message.

Report suspicious communication using the service's official support channel and your normal email or device reporting controls. For a company reviewing its own exposure, this case illustrates why account deletion and marketing-data retention need separate questions. Ask which provider holds historical contact records, what the retention policy covers and how a deletion request propagates to that provider. These are review questions, not a claim about the current Mindbox configuration.
The available description does not give the exact intrusion mechanism, so this article leaves that cause unresolved.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Geographic locations
fields.why: Where the account was used, which narrows a person down further than most people expect.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Genders
fields.why: Small on its own; useful to anyone assembling a fuller profile.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is about 12% of the population of Australia.
